_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Mathematics unit lecture film, Ask, Count and Chart. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. One survey runs through the whole film, and it is the lesson's own: How do the children in this class travel to school - Walk 9, Bus 6, Bicycle 4, Car 3, twenty-two children. The tally, the bar chart and the spoken numbers all describe that one count. The pictogram is the lesson's fruit survey with its key at two children a picture; the Venn and Carroll are the lesson's own even / more-than-twenty test with 8, 33, 24 and 7; the spinner is the lesson's own, three parts red, two blue, one gold.
title: Ask, Count and Chart
subtitle: Grade 3 Mathematics
objectives: Conduct an investigation to answer non-statistical and statistical questions (categorical and discrete data).

Record, organise and represent categorical and discrete data. Choose and explain which representation to use in a given situation: Venn and Carroll diagrams tally charts and frequency tables pictograms and bar charts.
Interpret data, identifying similarities and variations, within data sets, to answer non- statistical and statistical questions and discuss conclusions.
Use familiar language associated with chance to describe events, including ‘it will happen’, ‘it will not happen’, ‘it might happen’.
Conduct chance experiments, and present and describe the results.

beats.say: Some questions you cannot answer out of your own head.
You have to ask, count, and chart what people say.
Some questions you can just answer. Some need data.
How many legs has a spider? Eight, and everybody says eight.
Nobody knows how we travel to school until you ask us all.
Those answers vary - worth asking.
A tally counts things while they are still happening.
One mark for each child who walks. One, two, three, four.
The fifth mark lies across the other four, like a gate.
Now count the bundles in fives, then the ones left over.
One bundle is five, and four more makes nine children.
Write it in a table too. That is a frequency table.
A pictogram shows counts as pictures. Read the key: one picture means two children.
Apples has five pictures. Five twos make ten children.
Counting the pictures gives five, and five is the wrong answer.
Oranges has one picture and a half: two and one make three.
The same counts, drawn as bars. Taller bar, more children.
Along the bottom is each way. Up the side is how many.
Walk is the tallest bar, at nine. Car is shortest, at three.
Nine take away three is six. Altogether, twenty-two children answered, six more by walking than by car.

at.class: six more by walking than by car

beats.say: Sometimes you sort things instead of counting them.
Two hoops: even numbers in one, more than twenty in the other.
Eight is even, but not more than twenty. It goes in the even hoop.
Thirty-three is more than twenty, but it is odd. The other hoop.
Twenty-four is both, so it goes in the middle, where they overlap.
Seven is neither. A Carroll diagram gives it a box of its own.
There are many ways to show it. Choose one, and say why.
Not everything can be counted. Some things only might happen.
The sun will come up tomorrow. That one will happen.
You will not roll a seven on an ordinary dice. It has no seven.
A coin might land on heads. Might is not the same as will not.
Spin the arrow thirty times and keep the score as you go.
Red sixteen, blue nine, gold five. Red has the most room.
Ask a question whose answers vary, then count with a tally.
Read a pictogram by its key, and a bar chart by its height.
Sort with hoops or boxes. Some things only might happen.
